title: Why Adult Children Are Cutting Off Their Parents
author: Neil Shenvi
summary: Neil Shenvi reviews Noelle Mering's No Contact, which examines the growing trend of adult children severing all ties with their parents over grievances as minor as political disagreement. Shenvi highlights Mering's interviews, including a son who cut off his mother over a suspected vote and a daughter who stopped speaking to her father over his tepid response to a sibling's gender transition, and notes the unresolved grief such estrangement inflicts. He summarizes Mering's five drivers: identity politics, the demythologization of the family, therapeutic culture, the infallibility of victimhood, and cultural narcissism, with particular attention to how 'trauma' has expanded to cover ordinary childhood discomfort and how online estrangement coaches treat a child's impressions as unchallengeable. Citing Cato and PRRI surveys, he agrees that the pattern skews toward progressives and traces its ideas to the critical tradition of Marx and Marcuse. He endorses Mering's practical advice on building positive memories and listening well, but adds that some political commitments do reveal character, arguing that a shared need for grace should produce gentleness in disagreement.
points: Mering identifies five forces behind estrangement: identity politics, demythologizing the family, therapeutic culture, infallible victimhood, and cultural narcissism.
The concept of 'trauma' has expanded from catastrophic events to unmet emotional needs and political difference, and lived-experience claims are treated as beyond challenge.
Survey data cited in the review (Cato 2021, PRRI 2024) suggest strong liberals are far more likely than conservatives to cut off or reduce time with family over politics.
Mering's practical counsel for parents includes building a storehouse of positive memories, parenting for the child's actual world, wariness of social media, and listening to understand.
Shenvi adds that politics can reveal character, yet the recognition that all are sinners should make Christians gentle and humble across disagreements.
quotes: Gone are the days when family estrangement was a desperate, last resort of children who suffered through years of abuse and neglect under volatile, violent caregivers. In increasing numbers, adult children are disowning their parents, cutting off all communication and refusing any attempt at reconciliation, over nothing more serious than differences in political opinions.

When young adults break off contact with their families, it often imposes a huge emotional toll on the basis of seemingly minor infractions. One man cut his mother off because he suspected she voted for the wrong candidate. Another woman stopped communicating with her father because he was insufficiently enthusiastic about her sister’s gender transition.

Historically, “trauma” referred to serious psychological injury resulting from “extraordinary, catastrophic events like combat or surviving a train crash.” People now use the term to describe the discomfort experienced due to “political differences or unmet emotional needs” (18–19). Unpleasant but normal childhood experiences are now being labeled “trauma” and used to justify disowning parents. Though claims of trauma may seem exaggerated, they’re deemed indisputable because they’re validated as a person’s lived experience.

The cultural deconstruction of the family also plays a role in people’s willingness to sever connections. The family isn’t seen as a source of identity, growth, and stability but as a site of constraint, conformity, and oppression. Amid a culture seeking unbridled autonomy and individual self-expression, the family is a scandalous affront to one’s absolute sovereignty.

However, a 2021 Cato Institute survey found that “strong liberals” were almost twice as likely to “block/unfriend” and more than twice as likely to report someone over a social media post than “strong conservatives.” Likewise, a 2024 PRRI survey found that 23 percent of Democrats versus 5 percent of Republicans reported they would spend “less time with certain family members over their political views.” It tends to be political progressives who separate themselves from family members who don’t agree.
Consequently, prevention is key. Christian parents must train their children to recognize and reject ideologies fundamentally incompatible with the Bible’s vision of human identity, justice, and sin.

Apart from worldview considerations, parents can strengthen their relationship with their children in other ways. Mering urges families to “create a storehouse of positive memories,” to “parent for the world [the] children live in, not the one [the parents] grew up in,” to beware social media, and to listen to understand rather than to critique (229).

The very moral law that rightly undergirds our politics as Christians also condemns us as lawbreakers. The person who gets politics right and the person who gets politics wrong are both sinners who stand in need of the gospel. This recognition should produce a profound gentleness and humility, both in our private relationships and in the public square. Our common need for God’s grace is what allows us to love those with whom we disagree on important issues.
